Glitterati is a word used to describe the group of people who are famous, wealthy, glamorous, and highly visible in public life. Think of movie stars, fashion icons, socialites, celebrity musicians, high-profile athletes, and the super-rich who love being seen — the kind of people who show up at red carpets, exclusive parties, film festivals, fashion weeks, and charity galas, always looking dazzling, always being photographed.

The word paints a picture of a glittering social world — one full of designer clothes, flashy events, expensive champagne, and nonstop media attention. The people who belong to this world are the glitterati.

One important grammatical note: glitterati is always used as a plural noun. You would never say "a glitterati" referring to one person, just like you wouldn't say "a people." It always refers to the collective — the whole sparkling crowd of them together.

✅ "The glitterati descended on the Cannes Film Festival."
❌ "She is a glitterati."

This is where it gets nuanced, and understanding this will make you use the word with real precision.

The glitterati are not just any rich people, and not just any famous people. The word specifically applies to people who tick multiple boxes at once:

  • Famous or celebrated — people who are widely recognized
  • Wealthy or privileged — they live in a world of luxury
  • Glamorous — their image, appearance, and lifestyle are polished and dazzling
  • Socially visible — they actively participate in (or are naturally drawn into) the world of high-profile public events and social scenes

A quiet billionaire who hates cameras and lives on a farm away from the public eye is not glitterati. A Nobel Prize-winning scientist who is famous but has no interest in glamour or social scenes is not glitterati either. The "glitter" part matters deeply — these are people who shine in public, who are part of the spectacle, who are seen.
The Tone: Admiration With a Wink

The word glitterati is not completely neutral. It carries a slightly playful, tongue-in-cheek tone — like someone raising an amused eyebrow. When a writer uses "glitterati," there is usually a hint of one of two things (sometimes both):

  1. Admiration — for the glamour, the dazzle, the spectacle of it all.
  2. Gentle mockery — a quiet acknowledgment that this world can be a bit superficial, obsessed with appearances, and self-congratulatory.

It is rarely used as a harsh insult, but it's also not entirely reverent. It occupies that witty middle ground — appreciating the spectacle while gently poking fun at it. This makes it a favorite word in entertainment journalism, gossip columns, and social commentary, where writers want to describe the celebrity world with color and a light touch of irony.

You'll most commonly encounter "glitterati" in:

  • Entertainment and celebrity journalism ("Hollywood's glitterati gathered for the Oscars.")
  • Fashion and lifestyle writing ("Milan Fashion Week drew the international glitterati.")
  • Social commentary about celebrity culture and the ultra-wealthy elite
  • Casual conversation when someone wants to describe that shiny, glamorous social class with a bit of flair

• "The charity gala was attended by the city's glitterati, all dressed in couture and dripping in jewels."
  • "She moved to Los Angeles dreaming of rubbing shoulders with the glitterati."
  • "The hotel lobby was full of glitterati — pop stars, actors, and socialites all mingling before the awards ceremony."
  • "The film festival is less about cinema these days and more about the glitterati showing off." ← (note the slight ironic edge here)

If you had to boil it all down: glitterati refers to the collective group of rich, famous, and glamorous people who inhabit the dazzling world of celebrity, high society, and public spectacle — described with a tone that is equal parts admiring and gently amused.
